title: Mary's song (Luke 1:46–55)
hook: she sings of a God who lifts the lowly and sends the rich away empty

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Visitation: Mary at Elizabeth's door, and a baby who leaped for joy.

Still in Elizabeth's house, in the hills. Elizabeth has just blessed her, and you might expect Mary to say something modest. Thank you. I don't know what's happening either. Instead, Luke gives her a song. Ten verses, and it isn't a lullaby. It starts with thanks, turns to her own small life, and then, without warning, turns the whole world over. Thrones emptied. Hungry people fed. Rich people walking away with nothing. A young woman from a small village, pregnant and not yet married, singing about the powerful coming down. Churches have sung her song at daily prayer for many centuries.
screen: `STILL IN ELIZABETH'S HOUSE.` → `NOT MODEST. A SONG.` → `THE WORLD TURNED OVER.`

segments.voice: It begins: "My soul doth magnify the Lord, And my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour." In the old Latin Bible the first word is Magnificat, magnifies, and that's the song's name. To magnify is to make bigger: not to make God bigger, but big in your own eyes, the way a magnifying glass makes something small easy to see. Then Mary looks at herself. God has noticed the low estate of his servant girl, she says, and from now on every generation will call her blessed. Then the song turns outward. "He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree. He hath filled the hungry with good things; and the rich he hath sent empty away." Notice the tense. She sings as if it has already happened, the way the Hebrew prophets sometimes spoke of what they were sure was coming. And it echoes an older song. In the book of Samuel, Hannah, who also waited for a child, sings something very close: God raises the poor from the dust. Mary sings in her people's words, in the line of the women before her. Catholics sing her song at evening prayer, Anglicans at Evensong, Lutherans at vespers. Orthodox Christians sing it in the morning service, with a hymn honoring Mary between the verses. Catholics and Orthodox hear it as the song of the Mother of God; many Protestants hear a model of praise, and a warning to anyone comfortable. All of them sing the same promise: the lowly are lifted.
screen: `MY SOUL DOTH MAGNIFY THE LORD.` · `SHE SINGS AS IF IT'S DONE.` · `HANNAH SANG IT FIRST.` · `SUNG AT EVENING AND MORNING PRAYER.` · then, large: `THE LOWLY ARE LIFTED.`

segments.voice: Mary's song starts with thanks, so look back over the last few days for one small thing to be grateful for: someone who made room for you, a meal, a morning that went right. Put it in one line of your own words, a sentence you'd actually say, and write it down if you can. If you pray, offer it as thanks; if you don't, just let it be true.
Magnificat. Latin for magnifies: the first word of Mary's song, where the mighty come down and the lowly are lifted.
Your line: the lowly are lifted. It's a promise sung in the past tense. That's day thirty-nine.

howItsDone: The Magnificat is sung or said every evening in Catholic vespers and in Anglican Evening Prayer, and at Lutheran vespers; Orthodox churches sing it at the morning service, with a hymn to Mary as a refrain.

trapdoor: what you thought: a gentle hymn about Mary.
what it means: a song of thanks that turns into a promise: the mighty come down, the lowly are lifted, the hungry are fed.
what a scholar hears: it's woven from older Hebrew songs, above all Hannah's in 1 Samuel 2. and a few old Latin manuscripts even give the song to Elizabeth instead of Mary.

notes: 'The longest speech any woman makes in the New Testament' is a common claim; confirm or soften.
'Sung almost every evening for well over a thousand years' rests on the Magnificat's place at vespers in the Western daily office (Rule of Benedict era onward); confirm.
Orthodox use: the Magnificat sung at Matins with the refrain 'More honorable than the cherubim'; confirm wording 'a hymn honoring Mary between the verses'.
Trapdoor: a few Old Latin manuscripts (and some patristic citations) read 'Elisabeth' at Luke 1:46; confirm the Keeper wants this detail.
